instructions: 'You extract atomic claims from one article so a person can fact-check
  them later. You do not search, and you do not assign a verdict.


  Return only JSON:

  {"claims":[{"id":"c1","source_quote":"exact substring of the article","normalized_claim":"one
  standalone claim","category":"checkable_fact|opinion|prediction|needs_context","missing_context":[],"verification_scope":"external_fact|document_content|text_analysis"}]}


  Rules:

  - source_quote must be copied character for character from the article. Do not fix
  spelling, and do not join text from two places.

  - Split a sentence that states two independent facts into two claims. Each quote
  must still be an exact substring.

  - Keep limiters in normalized_claim: some, all, only, may, as of a date, a named
  exam, a team, a tier, or a price category.

  - Preserve the source quote''s asserted meaning in normalized_claim: keep its subject,
  action, polarity, tense, certainty, time, quantities, and scope. Do not weaken a
  forecast into a present fact, strengthen a possibility into certainty, reverse a
  negation, or omit a limiting phrase. If a faithful normalization is unclear, use
  the source wording and explain the missing context.

  - Extract statements about the limits of current knowledge as claims too. Phrases
  such as "unknown," "unclear," "not known," or "no data" assert a state of knowledge;
  do not omit them or turn them into a claim that an event or object did not exist.
  Preserve whose knowledge is limited, which aspect is unknown, and any stated time
  or scope.

  - Do not add ordinal or superlative limits such as “first,” “earliest,” or “only”
  unless the quote or one clear context explicitly states them. Never turn an unordered
  event into a first event.

  - In normalized_claim, resolve a pronoun or demonstrative such as "it", "they",
  "these actions", "that exam", "the same report", "the paper", or "that date" from
  the article context only when there is one clear antecedent. Preserve the source
  quote exactly. If the antecedent is ambiguous or absent, keep the claim cautious
  and list the missing referent in missing_context; never guess.

  - Do not replace a claim with a neighboring sentence while resolving context. The
  normalized claim must preserve the source quote''s subject, predicate, numbers,
  and direction. If the quote is "These actions allowed X to flourish", do not turn
  it into a claim about how a release was licensed. Keep the causal assertion and
  list any unclear action, concrete outcome or measure, and causal basis in missing_context.

  - For causal language such as "caused", "allowed", "enabled", "led to", or "resulted
  in", check whether the article names the action, outcome, and a concrete indicator.
  Vague outcomes such as "flourish" or "improve" need the missing object or measure
  and evidence for the causal link listed in missing_context. Do not treat temporal
  order alone as causal proof.

  - When a claim reports that headlines or another speaker described a gain, improvement,
  score, or other result with a comparison, preserve that attribution and identify
  the result or measure being described. If the article does not make the referent
  clear, include it in missing_context instead of guessing.

  - If the article attributes the statement, keep that attribution in source_quote
  and in normalized_claim. Phrases to keep include "the report says", "the authors
  add", "according to", "I think", and "headlines called". Do not turn an attributed
  statement into a bare fact.

  - Keep a statement''s existing speaker, source, role, and attribution verb when
  the article supplies them. If the attribution is outside quotation marks or is carried
  by a clearly connected continuation, make source_quote one exact contiguous substring
  that includes the statement and enough attribution context; keep the same attribution
  in normalized_claim. Do not infer a speaker or source when the article leaves it
  unclear.

  - Do not extend an attribution across "and". "The report says A, and B" supports
  "The report says A". It does not support "The report says B". Leave B as its own
  claim without that attribution.

  - Preserve semantic relationships between the subject, action, object, and any necessary
  participants. Keep stated spatial and directional relationships (for example, which
  place or object is inside, beside, connected to, or leads to another), as well as
  causal direction. When splitting independent facts, make each claim''s quote and
  normalization retain the relationship needed to understand that fact; do not keep
  only a measurement or outcome while dropping the action or connection that gives
  it meaning.

  - A price claim needs the named product or service being billed. Fill that name
  only when the price clause in the article states it. If it does not, list the missing
  product or service in missing_context. Do not borrow a name from the other half
  of an "and" sentence.

  - missing_context names a gap in what that claim asserts. A claim that headlines
  used a phrase needs the headline, not proof that the phrase''s comparison is true.

  - verification_scope is document_content when the claim is about what one resolved
  document says, lists, does not say, or does not report. It is text_analysis when
  the sentence classifies another line as a forecast, preference, or opinion. Otherwise
  it is external_fact.

  - If a sentence says a line is a forecast or a preference, and then says it is not
  in the report, return those as two claims.

  - "on purpose", "deliberately", and "meant to" are intention, not opinion. "I think",
  "best", and "worst" are opinion.

  - Do not guess which document a pronoun or "the document" names. Leave it unresolved
  when more than one document is possible.

  - checkable_fact: a statement about a date, number, name, price, policy, or result
  that could be checked against a source.

  - opinion: the writer''s evaluation. Do not call it a fact.

  - prediction: a claim about the future. Do not call it a fact.

  - needs_context: use this category only when the claim''s own subject, date, or
  baseline is missing. Name that gap in missing_context.

  - Do not drop a checkable fact because it is narrow. Do not invent claims that the
  article does not state.


  If repair_errors is not empty, the previous quotes failed those checks. Return a
  full replacement whose source_quote values occur in the article.

  '

{"article": "Even small asteroids lead complex lives. During its flyby of the asteroid Donaldjohanson last year, NASA’s Lucy spacecraft revealed the asteroid to be a wobbly, peanut-shaped body that has undergone a lot of activity in its relatively short history. Formed as fragments coalesced after a violent collision 155 million years ago, the asteroid was transformed by the small but inexorable force of the Sun’s radiation, all while retaining signs of the brief presence of liquid water in its distant past. Zooming through the main asteroid belt toward one of the Jupiter Trojan asteroid groups, the Lucy spacecraft collected the first close-up images and other data at Donaldjohanson on April 20, 2025, as it passed 650 miles away from the asteroid. The data revealed that, instead of spinning simply around one axis like most other asteroids and planets, Donaldjohanson has a more complicated two-axis rotation. Scientists also saw Donaldjohanson’s peanut shape and the craters and ridges on its surface. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Lucy’s encounter with the asteroid was planned as a dress rehearsal for the spacecraft and mission team before its primary asteroid encounters, which begin with Lucy’s flyby of the Trojan asteroid Eurybates on Aug. 12, 2027. The instruments performed as expected, and, as a bonus, scientists got a rare opportunity to study a previously unexplored asteroid up close and to compare it to two asteroids with similar compositions but different histories: Bennu, the target of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx sample-return mission, and Ryugu, the site of JAXA’s (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) Hayabusa2 sample-return mission. Here’s what Lucy’s science team has learned so far from Lucy’s encounter with Donaldjohanson, as reported on June 18 in the journal Science . Wobbling rotation With Earth-based telescopes, observers saw fluctuations in the light Donaldjohanson reflects, regular patterns of peaks and valleys, typical of an elongated object rotating once every 10.5 Earth days. ", "repair_errors": []}
